endorsements.quote: An integrated approach to build trust should include retrospective validation with local data (ie, test on your own data to trust it) and prospective evaluation using AI in practice.
As such, few clinicians trust AI for autonomous evaluation, and AI deployment strategies must incorporate radiologist supervision for the near future.
One way to facilitate the adoption of AI is to use model cards, which describe an AI model\u2019s purpose, usage, and limitations (85).

New metrics would be useful to measure AI\u2019s impact on workflow efficiency, assess clinical outcomes in radiology and related fields, and conduct randomized clinical trials to assess the utility of AI algorithms (55).

Radiologists should learn how to evaluate, interpret, and apply AI algorithms for tasks such as segmentation, detection, and classification, as well as how to handle and report imperfect algorithms (82).
AI must be easy to use within familiar software and compatible with the clinical workflow.
AI tools within PACS provide an efficient method for radiologists to adapt them into clinical practice.

unlisted_practices: Continuously monitor AI model performance, identify performance changes, and provide detailed, updated documentation.
Do not implement AI methods whose predictions are not repeatable, do not generalize within their development scope, or are not well calibrated.
Record and make available all details of the annotation process, including adjudication and quality assurance methods, to those evaluating AI tools for clinical deployment.
Clearly disclose the bias and limitations of in-house models that are not applicable to underrepresented populations.
Build diverse development and deployment teams to help identify and address bias in AI.
Integrate AI training for radiologists into early career curriculum.
Monitor deployment of models expected to have superhuman performance, such as long-term risk prediction, carefully.
Perform outcome prediction only in clinical scenarios where it has the potential to change care.
Organize design, development, deployment, and monitoring of radiology AI tools as collaboration between data scientists, software engineers, PACS specialists, and radiologists.
Prioritize data flow from acquisition devices to PACS, data lakes, and AI servers.
Focus validation on new images after scanner replacement or protocol change when reference standard data are unavailable.
Encourage communication between radiologists and AI scientists through grants, conferences, and gatherings to build trust.
Subject vision and language models to regulatory oversight.

screen.reason: Expert consensus/perspective paper from RSNA and MICCAI panels discussing considerations and recommendations for deploying AI in radiology.
